claim: Age is the main risk factor for Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and most neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Age is the main risk factor for Alzheimer's Disease (AD) and most neurodegenerative diseases. However, the mechanisms underlying this association are still poorly understood (Fjell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fjell et al., 2014, which provides scholarly support for this statement.

claim: Both normal aging and AD are associated with region-specific cerebral morphological changes characterized by the occurrence of atrophy.
source: Both normal aging and AD are associated with region-specific cerebral morphological changes characterized by the occurrence of atrophy (Bakkour et al., 2013; Fjell et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bakkour et al., 2013 and Fjell et al., 2014.

claim: Both aging and AD have differential and partially overlapping effects on specific regions of the cerebral cortex like the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Both aging and AD have differential and partially overlapping effects on specific regions of the cerebral cortex like, for instance, the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Bakkour et al., 2013; Fjell et al., 2014; Pichet Binette et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bakkour et al., 2013, Fjell et al., 2014, and Pichet Binette et al., 2020.

claim: Some brain regions are predominantly affected by age (e.g. calcarine cortex) and some others are predominantly affected by AD (e.g. medial temporal cortex).
source: Conversely, some regions are predominantly affected by age (e.g. calcarine cortex) and some others are predominantly affected by AD (e.g. medial temporal cortex; Bakkour et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bakkour et al., 2013.

claim: Machine learning techniques have gained popularity as brain-age prediction models due to their ability in identifying relevant data-driven patterns within complex data.
source: Recently, machine learning techniques have gained popularity as brain-age prediction models (Cole et al., 2017b; Dafflon et al., 2020; de Lange et al., 2019; Franke and Gaser, 2019), due to their ability in identifying relevant data-driven patterns within complex data (Zhavoronkov et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cole et al., 2017b, Dafflon et al., 2020, de Lange et al., 2019, Franke and Gaser, 2019, and Zhavoronkov et al., 2019.

claim: Higher brain-age deltas have been found in AD and individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) with respect to cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals.
source: Recent literature has shown the adequacy of using a brain-age predicted measurement in the assessment of the clinical severity of AD, by finding higher brain-age deltas in AD and individuals with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) with respect to cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals (Beheshti et al., 2018; Kaufmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beheshti et al., 2018 and Kaufmann et al., 2019.

claim: A higher brain-age delta has been reported in multiple sclerosis, epilepsy and psychiatric disorders with respect to healthy controls.
source: A higher brain-age delta has also been reported in other diseases, such as multiple sclerosis, epilepsy and psychiatric disorders, with respect to healthy controls (Beheshti et al., 2018; Kaufmann et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Beheshti et al., 2018 and Kaufmann et al., 2019.

claim: Brain-age delta has been associated with lifestyle factors, cognition, hypertension and prediction of mortality.
source: In addition, brain-age delta has also been associated with other biological measures such as: lifestyle factors (Cole, 2020), cognition (Beheshti et al., 2018; Cole, 2020) hypertension (de Lange et al., 2020a) and prediction of mortality (Cole et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cole, 2020, Beheshti et al., 2018, de Lange et al., 2020a, and Cole et al., 2018.

claim: The AD research framework criteria defines AD as a biological construct, namely the presence of both abnormal Aβ (A+) and tau (T+) biomarkers, regardless of clinical manifestations.
source: This is a very relevant aspect since the recent AD research framework criteria defines AD as a biological construct, namely the presence of both abnormal Aβ (A+) and tau (T+) biomarkers, regardless of clinical manifestations (Jack et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jack et al., 2018.

claim: Brain-age delta was recently associated with plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration and with imaging biomarkers of cerebrovascular disease in the 1946 British Birth Cohort.
source: Brain-age delta was recently associated with plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration and with imaging biomarkers of cerebrovascular disease in the 1946 British Birth Cohort Wagen et al., 2022; however, it was not associated with CSF biomarkers of neurodegeneration (Millar et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wagen et al., 2022.

claim: Brain-age delta was not associated with CSF biomarkers of neurodegeneration in the 1946 British Birth Cohort.
source: Brain-age delta was recently associated with plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration and with imaging biomarkers of cerebrovascular disease in the 1946 British Birth Cohort Wagen et al., 2022; however, it was not associated with CSF biomarkers of neurodegeneration (Millar et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Millar et al., 2022.

claim: Brain-age delta was significantly associated with AD biomarkers of amyloid and tau in MCI individuals, but these associations were not found in CU individuals.
source: Moreover, although brain-age delta was significantly associated with AD biomarkers of amyloid and tau in MCI individuals, these associations were not found in CU individuals (Millar et al., 2022; Wagen et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Millar et al., 2022 and Wagen et al., 2022.

claim: CU Aβ+ individuals had a higher brain-age delta than CU Aβ- individuals when the brain-age prediction model was trained in individuals with Aβ pathology.
source: Conversely, Another study focusing on the impact of training the brain-age prediction model in individuals with Aβ pathology (Aβ+) showed that CU Aβ+individuals had a higher brain-age delta than CU Aβ- individuals (Ly et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ly et al., 2020.

claim: Female individuals have a higher AD prevalence compared to males.
source: Moreover, given that female individuals have a higher AD prevalence compared to males (Nebel et al., 2018) and display different lifetime trajectories in the brain morphological features (Gennatas et al., 2017), it is of interest to determine the effect of sex on brain age delta and its interaction with AD biomarkers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nebel et al., 2018.

claim: Females and males display different lifetime trajectories in brain morphological features.
source: Moreover, given that female individuals have a higher AD prevalence compared to males (Nebel et al., 2018) and display different lifetime trajectories in the brain morphological features (Gennatas et al., 2017), it is of interest to determine the effect of sex on brain age delta and its interaction with AD biomarkers.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gennatas et al., 2017.

claim: Females with abnormal Aβ who are APOE-ε4 carriers show greater subsequent increase in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau than their male counterparts.
source: Literature describes sex differences in AD biomarkers, such as that females with abnormal Aβ who are APOE-ε4 carriers show greater subsequent increase in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau than their male counterparts (Buckley et al., 2019), or that females with higher Aβ burden show higher entorhinal cortical tau than their male counterparts (Buckley et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buckley et al., 2019.

claim: Females with higher Aβ burden show higher entorhinal cortical tau than their male counterparts.
source: Literature describes sex differences in AD biomarkers, such as that females with abnormal Aβ who are APOE-ε4 carriers show greater subsequent increase in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) tau than their male counterparts (Buckley et al., 2019), or that females with higher Aβ burden show higher entorhinal cortical tau than their male counterparts (Buckley et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Buckley et al., 2019.

claim: Levels of the neurodegeneration biomarker CSF neurofilament light (NfL) have been widely reported to be higher in males than in females.
source: Conversely, levels of the neurodegeneration biomarker CSF neurofilament light (NfL) have been widely reported to be higher in males than in females (Mielke, 2020; Milà-Alomà et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mielke, 2020 and Milà-Alomà et al., 2020.

claim: AD risk factors have been associated with greater brain aging in women than men.
source: For instance, AD risk factors have been associated with greater brain aging in women than men (Sanford et al., 2022; Subramaniapillai et al., 2021) and a lower brain aging has been found in the lower in the prefrontal cortex and insula in females (Sanford et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Sanford et al., 2022 and Subramaniapillai et al., 2021.

claim: A lower brain aging has been found in the prefrontal cortex and insula in females.
source: For instance, AD risk factors have been associated with greater brain aging in women than men (Sanford et al., 2022; Subramaniapillai et al., 2021) and a lower brain aging has been found in the lower in the prefrontal cortex and insula in females (Sanford et al., 2022).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sanford et al., 2022.

claim: The average prediction accuracy of the model run on UK Biobank using 10-fold cross-validation was MAE = 4.19 and R=0.71.
source: The average prediction accuracy of the model run on UK Biobank using 10-fold cross-validation as measured by the mean absolute error (MAE) and by Pearson's correlation were MAE = 4.19 and R=0.71 (Table 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the model performance evaluation and references Table 3 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Brain-age delta was higher in MCI with respect to CU individuals (PFDR <0.001).
source: Brain-age delta was higher in MCI with respect to CU individuals (PFDR <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: In both CU and MCI, a higher brain-age delta was significantly associated with abnormal Aβ status (CU: PFDR <0.001 and MCI: PFDR <0.001).
source: In both CU and MCI, a higher brain-age delta was significantly associated with abnormal Aβ status (CU: PFDR <0.001 and MCI: PFDR <0.001) and with progressive AT stages (CU: PFDR <0.001 and MCI: PFDR <0.001) (see Table 4 and Appendix 1—table 9 for more details).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Table 4 and Appendix 1—table 9.

claim: Brain-age delta was significantly associated with progressive AT stages (CU: PFDR <0.001 and MCI: PFDR <0.001).
source: In both CU and MCI, a higher brain-age delta was significantly associated with abnormal Aβ status (CU: PFDR <0.001 and MCI: PFDR <0.001) and with progressive AT stages (CU: PFDR <0.001 and MCI: PFDR <0.001) (see Table 4 and Appendix 1—table 9 for more details).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Table 4 and Appendix 1—table 9.

claim: The brain-age effect on AT stages was progressive, as that of the A+T- group was larger than that of A-T-, while the brain-age delta of A+T+ was larger than those of the other two previous stages.
source: The brain-age effect on AT stages was progressive, as that of the A+T- group was larger than that of A-T-, while the brain-age delta of A+T + was larger than those of the other two previous stages (Table 4 and Figure 3a).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Table 4 and Figure 3a.

claim: Brain-age delta was significantly associated with APOE status (CU: PFDR = 0.002 and MCI: P=0.017, PFDR = 0.040).
source: Brain-age delta was also significantly associated with APOE status (CU: PFDR = 0.002 and MCI: P=0.017, PFDR = 0.040).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: APOE-ε4 carriers had larger brain-age deltas compared to APOE-ε33 individuals for both CU (β=0.173, PFDR = 0.003) and MCI (β=0.273, PFDR = 0.008).
source: In particular, APOE-ε4 carriers had larger brain-age deltas (i.e. older-appearing brains than expected for their chronological age) compared to APOE-ε33 individuals for both CU (β=0.173, PFDR = 0.003) and MCI (β=0.273, PFDR = 0.008; see Table 4 and Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Table 4 and Figure 3.

claim: The positive associations between brain-age deltas and plasma NfL were significant within the CU (β=0.154, PFDR = 0.003) and MCI individuals (β=242, PFDR <0.001).
source: The positive associations between brain-age deltas and plasma NfL were significant within the CU (β=0.154, PFDR = 0.003) and MCI individuals (β=242, PFDR <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: CSF NfL was not significantly associated with brain-age delta (β=0.079, PFDR = 0.209).
source: CSF NfL was not significantly associated with brain-age delta (β=0.079, PFDR = 0.209).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The association between the longitudinal change in the aging signature composite and brain-age delta was not statistically significant (β=0.053, PFDR = 0.415).
source: The association between the longitudinal change in the aging signature composite, which was obtained from the cortical thickness in aging-vulnerable regions, and brain-age delta was not statistically significant (β=0.053, PFDR = 0.415).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The associations between brain-age delta and plasma NfL were significant within the CU and MCI females (CU: β=0.191, PFDR = 0.003 and MCI: β=0.342, PFDR = 0.003), but not within the males (CU: β=0.110, PFDR = 0.217 and MCI: β=0.141, PFDR = 0.137).
source: The associations between brain-age delta and plasma NfL were significant within the CU and MCI females (CU: β=0.191, PFDR = 0.003 and MCI: β=0.342, PFDR = 0.003), but not within the males (CU: β=0.110, PFDR = 0.217 and MCI: β=0.141, PFDR = 0.137).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: A significant interaction effect of age and CU brain-age delta on CSF NfL (Pinteraction_FDR<0.001) was found within the CU individuals, by which the measures of CSF NfL were higher with age and with larger brain-age deltas.
source: We found a significant interaction effect of age and CU brain-age delta on CSF NfL (Pinteraction_FDR<0.001) within the CU individuals (Figure 5a), by which the measures of CSF NfL were higher with age and with larger brain-age deltas (older-appearing brain).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Figure 5a.

claim: When stratifying by sex, the interaction effect of age on CSF NfL was seen in females (Pinteraction_FDR<0.001), but not in males (Pinteraction_FDR=0.393).
source: When stratifying by sex, this interaction effect of age was seen in females (Pinteraction_FDR<0.001), but not in males (Pinteraction_FDR=0.393).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: In both CU and MCI, brain-age delta was significantly associated with WMH (CU: β=0.160, PFDR <0.001 and MCI: β=0.222, PFDR <0.001).
source: In both CU and MCI, brain-age delta was significantly associated with WMH (CU: β=0.160, PFDR <0.001 and MCI: β=0.222, PFDR <0.001) (see Table 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Table 4.

claim: Brain-age delta was positively associated with WMH both in CU females (β=0.263, PFDR <0.001) and CU males (β=0.179, PFDR <0.001).
source: When studying the association between brain-age delta and WMH stratified by sex (Table 5) we found that the brain-age delta was positively associated with WMH both in CU females (β=0.263, PFDR <0.001) and CU males (β=0.179, PFDR <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Table 5.

claim: Brain-age delta was positively associated with WMH in MCI males (β=0.300, PFDR <0.001), but not in females (β=0.158, PFDR = 0.133).
source: Conversely, we found that the brain-age delta was positively associated with WMH MCI males (β=0.300, PFDR <0.001), but not in females (β=0.158, PFDR = 0.133).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Brain regions with highest SHAP values for both females and males included the volumes of the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, cerebellar white matter, lateral ventricles and the insula, as well as the cortical thickness of the superior-temporal cortex.
source: There were regions whose SHAP values were high in both females and males, including the volumes of the amygdala, nucleus accumbens, cerebellar white matter, lateral ventricles and the insula, as well as the cortical thickness of the superior-temporal cortex.
evidence: The claim is supported by SHAP analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The thickness of regions such as the transverse temporal cortex, the pars triangularis, the inferior parietal cortex and the left frontal pole thickness, as well as the volume of the left entorhinal cortex had higher SHAP values in females than in males.
source: Conversely, the thickness of regions such as the transverse temporal cortex, the pars triangularis, the inferior parietal cortex and the left frontal pole thickness, as well as the volume of the left entorhinal cortex had higher SHAP values in females than in males, while the opposite occurred with the thickness of the left isthmus cingulate and the right cuneus and the cortical volume of the superior frontal and right rostral middle regions (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by SHAP analysis results and references Figure 2c.

claim: The thickness of the left isthmus cingulate and the right cuneus and the cortical volume of the superior frontal and right rostral middle regions had higher SHAP values in males than in females.
source: Conversely, the thickness of regions such as the transverse temporal cortex, the pars triangularis, the inferior parietal cortex and the left frontal pole thickness, as well as the volume of the left entorhinal cortex had higher SHAP values in females than in males, while the opposite occurred with the thickness of the left isthmus cingulate and the right cuneus and the cortical volume of the superior frontal and right rostral middle regions (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by SHAP analysis results and references Figure 2c.

claim: The bi-lateral superior frontal volumes decreased more over the years within males than females, with an interaction of sex with age (Pinteraction <0.001).
source: For example, the bi-lateral superior frontal volumes decreased more over the years within males than females. This result was seen as the interaction of sex with age (Pinteraction <0.001).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: An interaction effect of sex and age for the isthmus cingulate thickness (Pinteratcion <0.001) was found, by which the thickness of males decreased more over the years than from the females.
source: We also found an interaction effect of sex and age for the isthmus cingulate thickness (Pinteratcion <0.001), by which the thickness of males decreased more over the years than from the females.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: The association between brain-age delta and a larger proportion of A+T+ was only seen in CU females (β=0.431, PFDR = 0.008) but not in CU males (β=0.139, PFDR = 0.424).
source: However, although a higher brain-age delta was significantly associated with progressive AT stages both for females (CU: PFDR = 0.002 and MCI: PFDR <0.001) and males (CU: PFDR = 0.019 and MCI: PFDR <0.001), brain-age delta of A+T + was significantly larger than those of the other two previous stages (A-T- and A+T-) in CU females (β=0.431, PFDR = 0.008) but not in CU males (β=0.139, PFDR = 0.424).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Brain-age delta was only significantly associated with APOE status in CU males (PFDR = 0.028), while this association was not seen in CU and MCI females and MCI males.
source: Brain-age delta was only significantly associated with APOE status in CU males (PFDR = 0.028), while this association was not seen in the rest of subgroups (CU and MCI females and MCI males).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: NfL is a marker of neuro-axonal damage which can be measured both in CSF and in plasma.
source: With the aim of studying the associations between brain-age delta and neurodegeneration, we computed the associations with NfL, a marker of neuro-axonal damage (Khalil et al., 2018) which can be measured both in CSF and in plasma, and with longitudinal changes in the aging signature composite as marker of age-related brain atrophy.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2018.

claim: NfL is correlated with age throughout the lifespan and has a strong association with all-cause mortality in the elderly.
source: The particular use of NfL in this context is supported by its correlation with age throughout the lifespan, as well as its strong association with all-cause mortality in the elderly (Kaeser et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kaeser et al., 2021.

claim: The expected annual change of NfL in CU individuals whose mean age range was 65 years old is around 3.5%.
source: Even though we found NfL to be positively associated with chronological age in CU individuals, in line with previous studies (Beheshti et al., 2018; Kaufmann et al., 2019; Khalil et al., 2020; Milà-Alomà et al., 2020), the expected annual change of NfL in CU individuals whose mean age range was 65 years old is around 3.5% (Khalil et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khalil et al., 2020.

claim: Cortical thinning with age has been linked to loss of volume of the neuropil and other non-neuronal processes which are not necessarily implicated in neurodegeneration.
source: In this regard, it is worth noting that cortical thinning with age has also been linked to loss of volume of the neuropil and other non-neuronal processes which are not necessarily implicated in neurodegeneration (Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2020.

claim: The increase in WMH with age has been previously studied.
source: These results were expected, as the increase in WMH with age has been previously studied (Maniega et al., 2015) and it has been shown that individuals with high WMH burden display spatial patterns of atrophy that partially overlap with those of brain aging (Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020a; Habes et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maniega et al., 2015.

claim: Individuals with high WMH burden display spatial patterns of atrophy that partially overlap with those of brain aging.
source: These results were expected, as the increase in WMH with age has been previously studied (Maniega et al., 2015) and it has been shown that individuals with high WMH burden display spatial patterns of atrophy that partially overlap with those of brain aging (Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020a; Habes et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020a and Habes et al., 2016.

claim: WMH have been linked to cognitive dysfunction and dementia.
source: In addition, WMH have been linked to cognitive dysfunction and dementia (Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020b; Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020a; Maniega et al., 2015) and a potential pathway has been proposed, in which small vessel cerebrovascular disease affects cognition by promoting neurodegenerative changes (Rizvi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020b, Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020a, and Maniega et al., 2015.

claim: A potential pathway has been proposed in which small vessel cerebrovascular disease affects cognition by promoting neurodegenerative changes.
source: In addition, WMH have been linked to cognitive dysfunction and dementia (Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020b; Brugulat-Serrat et al., 2020a; Maniega et al., 2015) and a potential pathway has been proposed, in which small vessel cerebrovascular disease affects cognition by promoting neurodegenerative changes (Rizvi et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rizvi et al., 2018.

claim: The brain regions that had highest impact on the machine learning prediction were similar to regions previously mentioned in literature.
source: In our study, the brain regions that had highest impact on the machine learning prediction were similar to regions previously mentioned in literature (Arenaza-Urquijo et al., 2019; Bakkour et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arenaza-Urquijo et al., 2019 and Bakkour et al., 2013.

claim: There was an overlap between some of the selected regions and regions included in the aging signature for both females and males, such as the precentral sulcus, insula, superior frontal and rostral middle frontal regions.
source: We found an overlap between some of our selected regions and regions included in the aging signature for both females and males, such as the precentral sulcus, insula, superior frontal and rostral middle frontal regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with the aging signature regions.

claim: Some studies report age–sex interactions in volumes of certain brain structures.
source: In addition, the effect of sex on age-related changes in brain structure has also been studied in the recent years, with some studies reporting age–sex interactions in volumes of certain brain structures (Coffey et al., 1998; DeCarli et al., 2005), and others not finding such interactions (Greenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Coffey et al., 1998 and DeCarli et al., 2005.

claim: Some studies do not find age-sex interactions in volumes of certain brain structures.
source: In addition, the effect of sex on age-related changes in brain structure has also been studied in the recent years, with some studies reporting age–sex interactions in volumes of certain brain structures (Coffey et al., 1998; DeCarli et al., 2005), and others not finding such interactions (Greenberg et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Greenberg et al., 2008.

claim: Reduction in the superior-frontal, isthmus-cingulate and pars orbitalis regions was found within males and regions such as inferior-parietal, pars triangularis and paracentral within females.
source: In particular, we found reduction in the superior-frontal, isthmus-cingulate and pars orbitalis regions within males and regions such as inferior-parietal, pars triangularis and paracentral within females.
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis results presented in the manuscript.

claim: Most of the sex-specific regions were in concordance with previous studies.
source: Most of these sex-specific regions were in concordance with previous studies (Armstrong et al., 2019; Podgórski et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Armstrong et al., 2019 and Podgórski et al., 2021.

claim: In the WHIMS-MRI study, women under menopausal hormone therapy were associated with greater brain atrophy.
source: Sexual hormones such as estrogen, progesterone and androgen could play a role in brain atrophy Armstrong et al., 2019; in the WHIMS-MRI study (Resnick et al., 2009), women under menopausal hormone therapy were associated with greater brain atrophy.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Resnick et al., 2009.

claim: It has been proposed that estrogen and progesterone may play a protective effect in women.
source: Others, however, have proposed that estrogen and progesterone may play a protective effect in women (Armstrong et al., 2019; Green and Simpkins, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Armstrong et al., 2019 and Green and Simpkins, 2000.

claim: Females have higher chances of undergoing neurodegeneration and have showed to undergo faster cognitive decline than males.
source: These results were expected, as females have higher chances of undergoing neurodegeneration and have showed to undergo faster cognitive decline than males (Ferretti et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ferretti et al., 2018.

claim: It has been suggested that the menopausal drop of estrogen increases vulnerability to neurological events.
source: Although the role of sex hormones still needs to be clarified, it has been suggested that the menopausal drop of estrogen increases vulnerability to neurological events (Green and Simpkins, 2000; Maioli et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Green and Simpkins, 2000 and Maioli et al., 2021.

claim: Positive associations between NfL and WMH have been previously demonstrated, for both CU and MCI.
source: Positive associations between NfL and WMH have been previously demonstrated, for both CU and MCI (Osborn et al., 2018), and the different AD stages (Walsh et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Osborn et al., 2018 and Walsh et al., 2021.

claim: It has been proposed that WMH may reflect two different pathological pathways, one including amyloid aggregation and another including axonal injury.
source: Moreover, it has been proposed that WMH may reflect two different pathological pathways, one including amyloid aggregation and another including axonal injury (Osborn et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Osborn et al., 2018.

claim: Brain aging in males might be driven more strongly by the amyloid aggregation pathway, while brain aging in females might be driven more by the axonal injury pathway.
source: Our results may suggest that brain aging in males might be driven more strongly by the former pathway, while brain aging in females might be driven more by the latter one.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the differential associations of NfL and WMH with brain-age delta in males and females.

claim: The study trained a model to predict brain-age separately for females and males using machine learning on imaging-derived measures of cortical thickness, cortical volume, and subcortical volume from the UK Biobank cohort (N=22,661).
source: We trained a model to predict the brain-age separately for females and males, using machine learning on imaging-derived measures of cortical thickness, cortical volume, and subcortical volume from the UK Biobank cohort (N=22,661).
evidence: The claim describes the methodology used in the study.

claim: Brain-age was estimated in four independent cohorts: ALFA+ (N=380), ADNI (N=719), EPAD (N=808), and OASIS (N=407).
source: Using this model, we then estimated brain-age in four independent cohorts: ALFA+ (N=380), ADNI (N=719), EPAD (N=808), and OASIS (N=407).
evidence: The claim describes the cohorts used for validation in the study.

claim: The study validated brain-age delta as a non-invasive marker of biological brain aging in non-demented individuals with abnormal levels of biomarkers of AD and axonal injury.
source: These results validate brain-age delta as a non-invasive marker of biological brain aging in non-demented individuals with abnormal levels of biomarkers of AD and axonal injury.
evidence: The claim summarizes the main conclusion of the study based on the results presented.

claim: Correlation coefficients between chronological age and predicted brain-age were not different between cohorts (P>0.05, for all comparisons).
source: Correlation coefficients were not different between cohorts (P>0.05, for all comparisons, see Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: Correlations and fitting performance metrics were not significantly different between females and males (Pearson's r (William's test), P>0.05; RMSE (F-test) P>0.05).
source: Correlations and fitting performance metrics were not significantly different between females and males (Pearson's r (William's test), P>0.05; RMSE (F-test) P>0.05), see Appendix 1—table 6.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis results and references Appendix 1—table 6.

claim: SHAP values reflect the marginal contribution of each brain region to the brain-age prediction.
